opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important open questions right now, and my honest answer is that we don't really know yet. I'd be careful about assuming the visual world will just follow the same curve as language.

With language models, we got lucky in a sense. Text is already a highly compressed, human-curated representation of the world. Every token carries a lot of semantic meaning, and next-token prediction turned out to be an incredibly clean objective. So when you scale data, parameters, and compute, you get this beautiful, predictable power-law behavior.

Vision is different. Pixels are raw, high-dimensional, and extremely redundant. Most of what's in a video frame is not that informative: textures, lighting, noise. If you naively scale a model to predict pixels, a lot of compute goes into modeling details that don't matter for understanding the world. So the first question is: what is the right objective? What are we actually scaling? In language, the answer was obvious early on. In vision, I don't think we've converged. Is it pixel reconstruction, prediction in a latent space, contrastive learning, or something we haven't invented yet? The scaling behavior will depend heavily on that choice.

Second, there's the data question. People say we're running out of text data, and that's somewhat true. Visual data, by contrast, is practically unlimited. Every camera, every robot, every person walking around is generating it. So in principle, the ceiling for a vision-based world model could be much higher than for language. But quantity isn't the same as useful signal. Visual data has low information density per bit, so you may need orders of magnitude more of it to get the same kind of gains. The curve may be flatter at first, then potentially keep going much longer.

Third, and this is what I find most exciting: I don't think the end goal is measured by the same metrics. For language models, we look at perplexity or benchmark scores. For a world model, what we care about is whether it understands physics, space, causality, and whether it can plan and act. Those abilities might not emerge smoothly. You might see something closer to phase transitions, where a capability like object permanence or a 3D understanding suddenly clicks at a certain scale, or only when you have the right kind of embodied, interactive data.

So my view is that scaling will absolutely matter for visual intelligence, but it won't be a simple copy of the language-model playbook. Language is a shortcut, a projection of the world that humans already did the hard work of creating. A real world model has to learn from the world itself, and that's a harder, messier problem. That's also why I think there's still so much room for new ideas here rather than just bigger GPUs.

r001.rationale: The response describes text as compressed and semantically rich, but does not connect that representation to a roughly balanced ratio of training tokens to model parameters.

r002.rationale: The response says visual scaling will not be a simple copy of language-model scaling, and describes a potentially flatter curve, longer scaling range, and abrupt capability transitions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't know yet, and I'd be a little suspicious of anyone who claims they do. But I can tell you how I think about it.

With language, we got very lucky. Text is already a compressed representation. Humans spent thousands of years doing the compression for us—every sentence is the output of a brain that has already perceived the world, abstracted it, and encoded it into discrete tokens. So when you train a language model, you're learning from data that is extremely information-dense, and the scaling curves look clean because the signal-to-noise ratio is so high.

Vision is the opposite. Pixels are raw. A single frame of video might be a million values, and most of them are redundant—the sky stays blue, the wall stays a wall. So if you scale a visual model naively, you spend enormous compute learning to reconstruct things that don't carry much semantic content. That's why I think the scaling law for visual world models will look worse in the early regime if you measure it the wrong way—say, by reconstruction loss—and potentially much better if you measure it by what actually matters, which is understanding and prediction in a useful representation space.

That's really the core of what we've been pushing on: the question of representation. Should the world model predict in pixel space, or in a learned latent space? My bet is on the latter. If you get the representation right—something closer to how the brain abstracts a scene—then a lot of the compute goes toward learning dynamics, physics, causality, rather than texture. And then I think scaling becomes very favorable, because the amount of visual data in the world dwarfs the amount of text. We've basically exhausted high-quality text. We haven't come close with video.

There's one more difference I think about a lot. Language models benefit from the fact that the task—next token prediction—is almost perfectly aligned with how the data was generated. For vision, the "right" objective is less obvious. Is it next-frame prediction? Is it predicting what happens after an action? Is it predicting in a semantic embedding space? I don't think we've converged on the objective yet, and until we do, comparing scaling laws is a bit like comparing two curves where one of them hasn't been drawn.

So, to summarize: I expect the curve to look different in shape, probably slower to start, driven more by representation and objective design than by raw parameter count. But the ceiling could be higher, because the world contains far more information than what humans ever bothered to write down.

r001.rationale: The response says text is a compressed, information-dense representation, but it does not connect that to a roughly balanced ratio of training tokens to model parameters.

r002.rationale: It expects visual world models to scale differently: slower initially, with scaling driven more by representation and objective design than raw parameter count, and with a potentially higher ceiling.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s still an open question. We’ve seen very clear scaling behavior in language models, but for world models, we first need to agree on what we’re scaling and what we’re measuring. Is the goal to predict the next video frame, or to build a representation that helps an agent understand what will happen when it takes an action? Those objectives can lead to very different conclusions.

Video contains an enormous amount of information, but also a lot of redundancy. If you double the number of frames, you haven’t necessarily doubled the amount of useful experience. And a model can become better at predicting pixels without becoming proportionally better at understanding the physical world. So the representation and the training objective matter a great deal.

My intuition is that we will see scaling laws for visual world models, but I wouldn’t assume they’ll have the same shape or efficiency as those for language models. The exciting question is whether we can find an objective where improvements with scale translate reliably into better prediction, planning, and interaction. That’s the connection we still need to establish.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss language models’ representation of knowledge or a training-token-to-parameter ratio.

r002.rationale: The response says visual world models may have different scaling-law shapes or efficiency, but frames this as uncertain and does not predict a substantially different law.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s still an open question. We’ve seen very clear scaling behavior in language models, but I wouldn’t assume that a visual world model will follow exactly the same curve.

One challenge is defining what we’re scaling and what we’re measuring. With language, you have a fairly consistent training objective: predict the next token. For a world model, are we predicting pixels, learning a representation, or predicting what happens after an action? Those objectives can produce very different behavior. A model might get better at generating realistic video without getting equally better at understanding physical cause and effect.

Video also contains a lot of redundancy. More frames don’t necessarily mean more useful information. The diversity of situations, interactions, and actions could matter as much as the raw amount of data.

So my expectation is that scaling will matter a great deal, but the representation and learning objective will determine how effectively we can use that scale. The interesting test is whether more compute and data give us models that can predict and reason about unfamiliar situations—not just produce something that looks plausible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language-model scaling and training objectives, but does not attribute the token-to-parameter ratio to how language models represent knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response says the comparison is an open question and cautions against assuming the same curve; it does not predict that visual world models will follow a substantially different scaling law.
